name: The Ginkgo of Toul

location.address: Parc de l'Hotel de Ville, Rue de Rigny, 54200 Toul, France

access: Free, standing in the public Parc de l'Hotel de Ville in the town centre.
transport: Walkable from Toul town centre; no public transport needed.
container: new place: standalone. No published city within day-trip range (Nancy ~20km has no page). A single labelled 'Arbre remarquable de France' with a real park setting and a distinctive golden-autumn spectacle; borderline on the single-tree-destination test since a ginkgo alone may not justify a dedicated trip, but it is a genuine remarkable-tree label holder with an interesting history. Recommend holding as a candidate for a future Toul or Meurthe-et-Moselle micro-page rather than shipping solo; flag for a second opinion on the single-tree bar.
story:
An admiral is said to have brought this tree home in his luggage. Henri de Rigny was born in Toul in 1782, and both the town and the departmental tourist board credit him with carrying a cutting or a seed north from a ginkgo in Toulon around 1804. Neither cites a period document, so it stays strong local tradition rather than settled fact. The tree itself is not in doubt: 21.84 metres when it was measured for its label, and if that 1804 planting holds, somewhere near 220 years old.

That would make it an early one for France. Ginkgo biloba has no living relatives, reached European gardens only in the eighteenth century, and was still a botanical curiosity when this one went into the ground behind the town hall.

Mid-November is the fortnight Toul waits for. A ginkgo does not fade into autumn so much as switch: the whole crown goes gold, holds for days, then drops most of it in one windless morning. Local guides like to say the Ecole de Nancy designers took their cue from foliage like this, a line repeated often and sourced nowhere.

On 7 June 2015 it became the 375th tree in the country to carry the label Arbre remarquable de France. Nobody has published a girth for it. If you have had a tape around the trunk, tell us.

best_time.label: mid-November, when the whole crown turns gold at once

name: The Millennial Yew of Estry

location.address: Cemetery beside the church, Estry, 14410 Valdallière, Calvados, Normandy, France

access: Free, standing in the public cemetery next to the church; open to visitors at any time.
transport: No station nearby; reached by car, in the village of Estry, Calvados.
container: new place: standalone. No published French city nearby (Caen is roughly 40km/40+ minutes away, beyond the day-trip boundary). Passes the single-tree-destination test cleanly: repeatedly called the oldest tree in Normandy/France, a genuinely dramatic hollow trunk, free public access in a churchyard, and an official Remarkable Tree label. Suggest a new standalone place, 'The Millennial Yew of Estry' or similar.
story:
The cavity inside this yew is about 3.1 metres across, and local accounts have thirty people standing in it at once. That hollow is also why nobody can date the tree: there are no rings left to count. Estimates run from 1,000 years to 1,800, and the Pays de Vire tourist board settles on somewhere between 1,000 and 1,600, which is about as close as anyone honestly gets. It is repeatedly called the oldest tree in Normandy, and by some accounts in France.

What can be measured has been, three times over a century, and the figure keeps moving. The trunk was 10 metres round in 1894, 11.4 metres in 1990 and 11.55 metres when someone put a tape around it again in July 2009. A tree still adding girth at that age is a tree still working.

Two of its great limbs reach roughly 15 metres out from the trunk and are carried on cables. Its roots are said to run more than 30 metres, under graves on the far side of the cemetery, though that one is village lore rather than survey.

It stands in the churchyard at Estry, a village now folded into the commune of Valdalliere, free and open at any hour. The ARBRES association labelled it a Remarkable Tree in September 2009.

name: The Oak of Tombeboeuf

location.address: Rural field off the road toward Laperche, about 8km northwest of Tombeboeuf, Lot-et-Garonne, France (near GPS N44 32.788 E0 26.056)

access: On private agricultural land but described by the tourism board as remaining accessible to visitors; free, self-guided. It stands alone in an open field and is hard to find without directions; the tourist board publishes a contact (CPIE47, +33 5 53 88 83 30) for visitor guidance. No OSM access check done in this pass; recommend a follow-up before publishing given it is named private land.
transport: No public transport; reached by car, roughly 8km outside Tombeboeuf village.
container: new place: standalone. No published city nearby (Agen is roughly 50km away). A genuine Tree of the Year 2019 winner with real fame and a dramatic solitary silhouette; passes the single-tree-destination test on that basis, but the private-land access and 2022 fissure report should be rechecked before shipping. Recommend a short follow-up check (vitality, current access) before this goes further.
story:
In 2019 France gave its Tree of the Year title to an oak standing on its own in a field. It sits on high ground about eight kilometres outside Tombeboeuf, with no signpost and no path to it, which is why the departmental tourist board publishes a telephone number instead of directions.

The two accounts of the tree do not agree. The tourist board puts it at roughly 300 years, 6.30 metres round and 25 metres tall. A specialist tree blog that walked out to it in 2008 called it young at 250 and paid more attention to its shape: the first branches leave the trunk about three metres up and then travel sideways rather than up, which is what an oak does when nothing near it competes for light. The ARBRES association had already labelled it a Remarkable Tree in 2003.

Two things worth knowing before driving out. The field is private agricultural land, and the tourist board describes the tree as remaining open to visitors, which is not the same thing as a right of way. And a local report in May 2022 mentioned a worrying fissure in the trunk, which we have not been able to follow up. If you get there, tell us how it looks.

Nobody has settled which oak it is, either. If you can read the leaf, say so.

name: The Oak of the Virgin at Rannee

location.address: Roadside between La Guerche-de-Bretagne and Rannee, at the edge of the forest of La Guerche, Ille-et-Vilaine, France

access: Free, roadside/forest-edge location, no ticket or booking. Coordinate is the lead's own (from Commons/famous_trees.py, not independently re-verified against a mapped source this pass), so treated as approximate.
transport: Reached by car, about 45 minutes from Rennes.
container: new place: standalone, or possibly foldable into a future Rennes-area page if Rennes is ever opened (currently no published city in Ille-et-Vilaine). Passes the single-tree-destination test on the strength of its story and devotional tradition (a genuinely unique, continuously-visited shrine-tree) rather than on age or size; recommend a follow-up pass to pin the exact coordinate before shipping, since none was found here.
story:
In July 2018 one of the candles left at this oak set fire to it. The offerings were back the next day.

The trunk is covered from the base upward in small boxed statues of the Virgin, along with rosaries and ex-votos. By local tradition the first one was placed in 1792. Republican soldiers hunting a refractory priest during the Terror are said to have shot a young girl at the foot of the tree when she would not say where he was hiding, and the statuette she had put in a hollow of the trunk stayed there. People have been adding to it ever since. That is the story as this corner of Brittany tells it rather than anything a court record confirms, and the tradition is the verifiable part: the offerings are there, and they are replaced.

Both accounts of the fire agree the trunk survived it. How well the crown has recovered since is something a visitor can see better than we can.

What is missing is everything a register would hold. Nobody has published an age or a girth, and nobody has settled which oak this is. If you get there with a tape measure or a good eye for a leaf, tell us.

It stands at the roadside on the edge of the forest of La Guerche, free, at any hour, about 45 minutes out of Rennes.

name: Diane de Poitiers' Tree

location.address: Parc de Diane, Les Clayes-sous-Bois, Yvelines, France

access: Free, standing in the public Parc de Diane.
transport: Les Clayes-sous-Bois is served by Transilien line L from Paris Saint-Lazare, roughly 30-35 minutes; a short walk from the station to the park.
container: Possibly joins Paris (Transilien puts it at the edge of, or just past, the 30-minute day-trip boundary depending on the exact stop and walk time; worth an honest transport-time check before deciding). Otherwise stands alone: a real ARBRES-labelled remarkable tree with a dramatic natural-layering spectacle and a well-known (if legendary) royal association, which clears the single-tree-destination bar on its own.
story:
This plane tree is 31 metres tall and 43 metres wide, which is the wrong way round for a plane and takes some explaining. The explanation is at ground level. Low branches that reached the soil have rooted where they touched it and sent up growth of their own, a habit called layering, helped along by a pond close enough to keep the ground damp. The tree has been quietly walking outward for centuries.

It is named for Diane de Poitiers, mistress of Henri II, who is said to have had it planted around 1556. French Wikipedia files that as legend rather than documented fact, so take the name as a name and the date as a story: at face value it would make the tree about 470 years old. What nobody disputes is a trunk over eight metres round and a shape that took a very long time to build.

Oriental planes are the parent species of the London plane, the tree that lines half the boulevards of Europe, and they are far less often left alone long enough to do what this one has done. Most planes get pruned into a column. This one was allowed to sprawl.

The ARBRES association labelled it a Remarkable Tree in July 2000. It stands free and open in the Parc de Diane at Les Clayes-sous-Bois, west of Paris in the Yvelines, a short walk from the station.

name: The Great Linden of Argoules

location.address: Place du village, Argoules, Somme, France

access: Free, standing on the open village square (place du village) beside the church and chateau; no restriction.
transport: No station; reached by car, in the Baie de Somme area of the Somme department.
container: new place: standalone. No published city nearby in the Somme/Baie de Somme area. A genuinely labelled remarkable tree with real civic prominence (village square, namesake inn) and a good recovery story; passes the single-tree-destination test on its historical designation and setting.
story:
The storm of 15 and 16 October 1987 tore the crown clean off this lime. It has been rebuilding one ever since, slowly and under protective care, which is the plainest evidence anyone could ask for that the tree is still working.

Four hundred years is the figure the sources reach for, on the belief that it dates from the start of the seventeenth century. A competing local account makes it a liberty tree planted in 1792 or 1793, when villages across France were putting them in, which would roughly halve its age. Both sources flag these as rival stories rather than one settled date, so the honest answer is that Argoules does not know how old its lime is.

What the state decided is easier to pin down. The tree was classified as a botanical natural monument in 1934, and in 2016 it was labelled Arbre remarquable de France.

It stands on the open square between the Saint-Germain church and the chateau, in the Baie de Somme country, free and unfenced. The village inn is named after it, the Auberge du Gros Tilleul, which tells you how long it has been the thing people navigate by here. No girth figure has ever been published. If you bring a tape, we would like the number.

name: The Linden of Joncquoy
access: Free, standing beside the Chemin du Joncquoy, a short distance from the village; described by a hiking-route page (visorando.com) as a stop on an ordinary public walking route.
transport: No station; reached by car or on foot from Aubers village, in the Weppes area near Lille.
container: new place: standalone. No published city nearby (Lille has no page). A genuinely dramatic survivor story (war, lightning, fire, storm) with civic recognition (tourism office logo, national Tree of the Year nomination); clears the single-tree-destination bar easily.
story:
Shellfire levelled the village of Aubers in the First World War. This lime, standing apart from the houses, came through it.

That is only the most recent thing it has outlasted. A map of 1706 shows three more lindens on the same site, all of them long gone. The tree was reportedly split by lightning in 1721 and grew on regardless. The Chateau de Joncquoy and its Le Notre gardens, which stood here, both went in the Revolution, and this is the last living piece of that estate. It also took the storm of 1999, which flattened woodland across northern France, without going over.

A deed of 1490 is cited for the planting, which would put it past 530 years. It is 12 metres tall today and 5.1 metres round: low and thick rather than grand, which is roughly what five centuries of weather leave behind.

It was nominated for France's Tree of the Year in 2020, and the Weppes tourism office thought enough of it to put it on its own logo. You reach it on foot along the Chemin du Joncquoy, on an ordinary walking route out of the village, free and at any hour, with nothing between you and it.

name: The Oak of the Swedes

location.address: Beside the D662/road from Reyersviller toward Siersthal, Reyersviller, Moselle, France

access: Free, standing beside a public road at the edge of the village; no restriction.
transport: No station; reached by car, in the Pays de Bitche area of Moselle.
container: new place: standalone. No published city within day-trip range (Strasbourg is roughly 70km away). A genuinely dramatic wartime-atrocity legend attached to a real, visually striking veteran oak on a public roadside; clears the single-tree-destination bar on story and age together.
story:
Somebody fixed a small crucifix to this oak, and the reason given for it is the darkest story in the Pays de Bitche. Local tradition holds that during the Thirty Years' War, in 1633 or 1634, Swedish mercenaries hanged the entire population of a nearby hamlet called Kirscheidt from its branches when the villagers would not say where a treasure was hidden. Kirscheidt no longer exists. Nor does any contemporary record of the hanging: the story is repeated locally and in regional history writing, and it stays tradition rather than documented event.

The war behind it needs no such caution. Fighting, famine and plague emptied whole stretches of Lorraine in those years, and villages that went then stayed gone.

The specialists who have walked out to the tree put it somewhere between 400 and 500 years old. Take the older end of that range and it was already a century old when the mercenaries came through. Take the younger and it was a sapling barely in the ground. It stands about 20 to 21 metres, though one visit in 2012 recorded 25, and nobody has published a girth. The silhouette is twisted and storm-worn, the shape an oak takes after several centuries alone in the open.

It is at the roadside between Reyersviller and Siersthal, free, with nothing between you and the trunk.

name: The Millennial Yew of Yvignac-la-Tour

location.address: Beside the church, Yvignac-la-Tour, Cotes-d'Armor, Brittany, France

access: Free, standing beside the parish church; ordinary churchyard access.
transport: No station; reached by car, near Dinan in Cotes-d'Armor.
verify_notes: Believed to date from when a chapel on the site became the parish church, somewhere in the 7th to 11th century, so treat the 'thousand years' figure as the source's own loose estimate rather than a precise date; some local sources connect the Breton word 'if' (yew) to the town's own name. Girth 8.5m (850cm) measured at 1m height, per krapooarboricole's visit. The tree is hollow and visibly declining but still described as having 'a reasonably harmonious form'; the commune planted a successor yew beside it in December 2000, which is itself a sign the original was already recognised as failing over two decades ago and is being actively stewarded rather than neglected. Local tradition holds a refractory priest, Guillaume Gauvain (d.1794, French Revolution), is buried beneath its roots. No tree-level coordinate found in this pass; the lead's own lat/lng were null, and I could not confirm a coordinate against a mapped source, so location stays approximate (behind/beside the church only).
container: new place: standalone. No published city nearby (Dinan has no page). A genuinely ancient, well-documented churchyard yew with real local history (Revolutionary-era burial legend, name etymology); clears the single-tree-destination bar on age and story, though a follow-up should try to pin an exact coordinate and find a post-2010 condition check.
